cls: Selective irreversible monoamine oxidase type B (MAO-B) inhibitor
quick: 1 mg once daily (monotherapy); 0.5-1 mg once daily as adjunct to levodopa
With or without food; avoid high-tyramine foods at high exposures
Limited data; use only if clearly needed
May inhibit prolactin/milk; use with caution
No adjustment needed in renal impairment
0.5 mg daily in mild; avoid in moderate-severe impairment
Use caution; may add to CNS effects
Blood pressure, serotonin-syndrome signs, melanoma skin checks, dyskinesia
summary: Rasagiline is a selective, irreversible inhibitor of monoamine oxidase type B (MAO-B) used to treat Parkinson's disease as monotherapy and as adjunct to levodopa. By blocking MAO-B it reduces dopamine breakdown in the brain, improving motor symptoms. Important precautions include the risk of serotonin syndrome and hypertensive reactions with certain co-medications, a 0.5 mg dose in mild hepatic impairment, dose reduction with CYP1A2 inhibitors such as ciprofloxacin, and monitoring for melanoma.
indications: Treatment of Parkinson's disease as monotherapy
Treatment of Parkinson's disease as adjunct therapy to levodopa

dosage.d: 0.5 mg once daily, may increase to 1 mg once daily
dosage.n: Titrate up for sufficient clinical response
Do not use in moderate/severe impairment

admin: Take once daily, with or without food
When used as adjunct to levodopa, the levodopa dose may need reduction to limit dyskinesia
Reduce to 0.5 mg daily with concomitant CYP1A2 inhibitors
Allow a washout when switching from/to other MAO inhibitors or serotonergic drugs
At recommended doses dietary tyramine restriction is generally not required, but avoid very high-tyramine foods
moa: Rasagiline is a potent, selective, irreversible inhibitor of monoamine oxidase type B (MAO-B), the enzyme that metabolizes dopamine in the brain. By inhibiting MAO-B it increases extracellular dopamine levels in the striatum, enhancing dopaminergic transmission and improving the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease. Its selectivity for MAO-B over MAO-A lessens the tyramine ('cheese') reaction at therapeutic doses.

absolute: Concomitant use of other MAO inhibitors or linezolid (hypertensive crisis risk)
Concomitant dextromethorphan, St. John's wort, cyclobenzaprine
relative: Concomitant serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs) - serotonin syndrome risk
monitor: Serotonin syndrome features when serotonergic drugs unavoidable

preg: There are limited data in pregnant women. Use rasagiline during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: Animal data suggest rasagiline may inhibit prolactin secretion and could suppress lactation; excretion into human milk is not well characterized. Use with caution and monitor the infant if breastfeeding.
renal: No dosage adjustment is required in patients with renal impairment.
hepatic: Use 0.5 mg once daily in mild hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh A). Rasagiline should not be used in patients with moderate or severe (Child-Pugh B or C) hepatic impairment.

major: Other MAO inhibitors and linezolid - risk of hypertensive crisis; contraindicated
Meperidine, tramadol, methadone, propoxyphene - serotonin syndrome/serious reactions; contraindicated
Dextromethorphan - episodes of psychosis/bizarre behavior; avoid
Sympathomimetic amines (including nasal/oral decongestants, ephedrine) - hypertension
moderate: SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclic/tetracyclic antidepressants - serotonin syndrome; use lowest doses with caution or avoid
CYP1A2 inhibitors (ciprofloxacin) - increase rasagiline levels; reduce to 0.5 mg
Dopaminergic agents/levodopa - additive dyskinesia and hypotension
minor: CYP1A2 inducers (smoking) - may lower rasagiline levels
interactions.food: Avoid very high-tyramine foods (aged cheeses, cured meats, tap/unpasteurized beer) - hypertensive reactions can occur, especially at higher than recommended doses
interactions.alcohol: Use caution; may add to CNS depression and orthostatic effects
interactions.diagnostics: No specific laboratory interference; monitor blood pressure clinically

serious: Falls / somnolence and sudden sleep onset
rare: Melanoma (increased background risk in Parkinson's disease)
Withdrawal-emergent hyperpyrexia and confusion on abrupt discontinuation
emergency: Hypertensive crisis (severe headache, chest pain, visual disturbance)

monitoring: Blood pressure, including for orthostatic hypotension
Signs of serotonin syndrome if serotonergic agents are co-prescribed
Motor response, dyskinesia, and impulse-control behaviors
counsel: Tell every prescriber and pharmacist you take an MAO-B inhibitor before any new medicine
Avoid certain cold/cough remedies (dextromethorphan, decongestants) and the pain medicine meperidine/tramadol
Limit very aged cheeses and cured/fermented foods, and avoid large amounts of tyramine-rich food
Rise slowly from sitting/lying to avoid dizziness
Report severe headache, racing heart, fever with muscle stiffness, or new gambling/compulsive urges
Have skin checks for unusual moles or skin changes
pk: Rapidly absorbed; clinical motor benefit develops over days to weeks
Plasma peak (Tmax) approximately 1 hour after dosing
Plasma half-life ~1.3-3 hours, but MAO-B inhibition is irreversible and outlasts plasma levels
Effect persists until new MAO-B is synthesized (about 2 weeks), supporting once-daily dosing
Store at 25 C (excursions 15-30 C); protect from light and moisture
pearls: Selective irreversible MAO-B inhibitor - effect outlasts the short plasma half-life
At recommended doses strict tyramine-free diet is usually not required, but avoid very high-tyramine foods
Reduce to 0.5 mg daily with ciprofloxacin or other CYP1A2 inhibitors
Many serotonergic and opioid drugs (meperidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan) are contraindicated
Use only 0.5 mg in mild hepatic impairment and avoid in moderate-severe impairment
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and take the next one as scheduled - do not double up.
overdose: Overdose may produce effects ranging from those of MAO-A and MAO-B inhibition. Symptoms can include hypertension and postural hypotension, drowsiness, dizziness, and at high doses features resembling non-selective MAOI overdose (agitation, hyperthermia, autonomic instability). There is no specific antidote; manage supportively with blood pressure and temperature control.
